newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Recount shows Izetbegovic winning Bosnia poll.
newsitem.headline: Recount shows Izetbegovic winning Bosnia poll.

text.p: A recount in Bosnia's elections following errors and confusion during vote counting confirmed that President Alija Izetbegovic won the top job in a new collective presidency, organisers said on Sunday.

But the "preliminary final result" showing Izetbegovic narrowly beating Serb separatist Momcilo Krajisnik must still be re-verified by computer and opened to possible appeals before it can be officially certified, a process likely to take until next weekend, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe added.

The OSCE said on Saturday that many errors in the vote count had forced a recount and cross-check of margins in key races including the presidency, where Izetbegovic's "provisional" victory was announced last week.
Preliminary final results released on Sunday gave 731,024 votes to Izetbegovic, a Moslem, to 690,130 for Krajisnik, the ultra-nationalist speaker of parliament in Bosnia's separatist Serb entity.

Kresimir Zubak won the Croat seat on the tripartite presidency with 329,891 votes. The results confirmed provisional totals issued last week with a slight widening of Izetbegovic's margin over Krajisnik.

The elections were aimed at creating a union government reintegrating three communities divided by 43 months of war. The OSCE was due to have announced the final results on Saturday, a week after voting.

"We have tightened up our (counting) operation over the past few days. We have swept through all the data we received and were able to reconcile them, ensuring there were no duplicate entries (or) transposition of numbers," said OSCE election director Jeff Fischer.
He said final unofficial results would probably be issued on Tuesday after a final round of computer verification and then submitted to the OSCE's Provisional Election Committee for certification.
That would follow a 72-hour period for the lodging of appeals which must be ruled on by the OSCE within 72 hours of receipt.

Provisional results released earlier showed the main Moslem, Serb and Croat nationalist parties easily winning parliamentary races in their respective domains of Bosnia. Recounts and cross-checks were not expected to cancel nationalist majorities.
But they could mean the difference between parliamentary seats and the political wilderness for small opposition civic parties which campaigned for ethnic reconciliation in Bosnia.
The post-election disarray may cost peace coordinators momentum -- a crucial issue in view of early signs of obstruction by Serb separatists -- and erode the legitimacy of new governing institutions.
"You are giving the nationalist hardliners an excuse to challenge the authenticity of the entire process," said Hrair Balian of the International Crisis Group (ICG), a think tank.

Critics say the United States, which brokered Bosnia's peace treaty, was so keen to see the pro-unity Izetbegovic head the new presidency that the OSCE's American-run Bosnia mission declared him the winner last week based on unchecked results.
They point to indications of a voter turnout of 82 to 104 percent, astronomical by all but the standards of rigged communist bloc elections.
Only 74 percent turned out in 1990 Bosnia elections -- and this was before tens of thousands of people were killed and two million were displaced in a 43-month-long war.
